title: PostgreSQL Practical Data Types, JSONB, and Identity Columns
description: Master production PostgreSQL types: text, integer, numeric, boolean, timestamps, serial vs identity columns, native arrays, and semi-structured JSONB storage.
learning_objectives: Select appropriate PostgreSQL data types including text, integer, numeric, and boolean for production workloads
Manage temporal data correctly using timestamps with timezone awareness (TIMESTAMPTZ)
Implement modern SQL-standard generated identity columns over legacy serial sequences
Store and query semi-structured document payloads using JSON and JSONB with specialized operators and GIN indexing

sections.title: Core PostgreSQL data types: text, integer, numeric, and boolean
sections.learning_objective: Choose optimal scalar data types to guarantee precision and efficiency.
sections.markdown: Choosing the right `PostgreSQL data types` is foundational for data integrity and performance. For text, PostgreSQL's `text` and `varchar` types have identical internal storage; `text` without length limits is preferred unless business rules demand length constraints. For numbers, use `integer` (4 bytes, up to 2 billion) or `bigint` (8 bytes). For financial and monetary values, NEVER use floating point types; always use `numeric` (or `decimal`), which provides arbitrary exact precision without rounding inaccuracies. For logical flags, use `boolean` (`TRUE`, `FALSE`, or `NULL`).

examples.explanation: Defines typed attributes using exact numeric, integer, text, and boolean types.

key_points: Always use NUMERIC/DECIMAL for currency and financials to avoid IEEE-754 floating point drift.
In PostgreSQL, TEXT has no performance penalty compared to VARCHAR(N).
BOOLEAN supports true, false, and unknown (NULL).
sections.checkpoint: Why does calculating 0.1 + 0.2 with floating point numbers cause precision issues?

sections.title: Temporal types: Timestamps and timezone awareness
sections.learning_objective: Store and manipulate time values using TIMESTAMPTZ.
sections.markdown: PostgreSQL provides two primary timestamp types: `timestamp without time zone` (`TIMESTAMP`) and `timestamp with time zone` (`TIMESTAMPTZ`). In production engineering, always use `TIMESTAMPTZ` for events and logs. When saving a `TIMESTAMPTZ`, PostgreSQL converts the input string to UTC and stores it as an 8-byte UTC integer. When queried, it converts the UTC value back into the client session's timezone. Using `TIMESTAMP` (without timezone) discards offset context, leading to catastrophic scheduling and audit bugs across global services.

examples.explanation: Normalizes incoming timestamps across different time zones into a unified UTC timeline.

key_points: Always use TIMESTAMPTZ for application event logs, user actions, and timestamps.
TIMESTAMPTZ converts incoming offsets to UTC internally for uniform time comparisons.
sections.checkpoint: What happens if a client in Tokyo and a client in New York insert 'now()' into a TIMESTAMP column?

sections.title: Surrogate keys: Generated identity vs serial
sections.learning_objective: Implement SQL-standard GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY columns over legacy SERIAL.
sections.markdown: Historically, PostgreSQL used `serial` pseudo-types (`serial`, `bigserial`) to implement auto-incrementing primary keys. However, `serial` has major drawbacks: it creates a loosely coupled background sequence owned by the user, and manual inserts can easily desynchronize the sequence. In PostgreSQL 10+, use standard SQL `identity` columns: `id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY` or `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY`. Identity columns tie sequence ownership directly to the table, preventing permissions errors and accidental sequence desynchronization.

examples.explanation: Creates an auto-incrementing primary key using standard GENERATED AS IDENTITY.

key_points: GENERATED AS IDENTITY is the modern SQL-standard replacement for legacy SERIAL sequences.
GENERATED ALWAYS blocks manual ID insertions unless OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is specified.
sections.checkpoint: Why is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY safer than SERIAL against accidental manual key overrides?

sections.title: Semi-structured data: Arrays, JSON, and JSONB
sections.learning_objective: Store and query semi-structured data using native arrays and binary JSONB.
sections.markdown: PostgreSQL provides powerful support for non-scalar data. First, native `arrays` (`TEXT[]`, `INT[]`) allow storing lists of values with containment operators (`@>`, `&&`). Second, PostgreSQL supports `JSON` and `JSONB`. `JSON` stores raw text (requiring re-parsing on every query), whereas `JSONB` stores decomposed binary data, eliminating whitespace and duplicate keys. `JSONB` supports indexed lookups using GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes and operators like `->` (returns JSON) and `->>` (returns text).

examples.explanation: Demonstrates native array containment and JSONB key extraction.

key_points: Use JSONB rather than plain JSON for queryable semi-structured document payloads.
Use -> to extract nested JSON objects and ->> to extract values as SQL text.
GIN indexes on JSONB columns allow sub-millisecond document search queries.
sections.checkpoint: What is the difference in output type between payload->'user' and payload->>'user'?

sections.title: PostgreSQL practicals interview check and practice
sections.learning_objective: Master PostgreSQL specific questions in engineering interviews.
sections.markdown:
PostgreSQL specific questions test whether you understand real-world database administration and type nuances.

### Common Interview Questions
1. *When should you use JSONB instead of creating new relational tables?*
   *(Use JSONB for variable schema attributes, third-party webhook payloads, or dynamic configuration flags that change rapidly. Use relational tables for core business entities with foreign keys, transactional integrity, and predictable reporting needs).* 
2. *What is the difference between VARCHAR(255) and TEXT in PostgreSQL?*
   *(In PostgreSQL, they use the exact same underlying varlena storage engine. VARCHAR(255) merely adds a character length check. There is zero performance advantage to VARCHAR(255) over TEXT).* 
3. *How do you index a JSONB column efficiently?*
   *(Using a GIN index: `CREATE INDEX idx_meta ON table USING gin (metadata)`)*. 

### Arena Practice Problems
- `sql-age-from-birthdate`: Calculating date intervals and practical age transformations
- `sql-coalesce-address`: Handling null fallbacks with practical COALESCE expressions
- `sql-daily-sales`: Grouping and aggregating by date intervals

examples.code:
-- Querying JSONB with containment operator @>
SELECT id 
FROM model_configs 
WHERE parameters @> '{"model": "gemini-2.5"}';
examples.explanation: Uses GIN-indexable JSONB containment operator to find matching documents.

key_points: Always choose TIMESTAMPTZ over TIMESTAMP for application events.
Know the differences between JSON (stored as text) and JSONB (binary decomposed).
sections.checkpoint: What index type should you create on a JSONB column to support @> containment queries?

summary: PostgreSQL data types: TEXT is preferred over arbitrary VARCHAR(255); NUMERIC is mandatory for currency.
TIMESTAMPTZ converts incoming times to UTC for lossless storage and timezone-aware querying.
GENERATED AS IDENTITY provides standard SQL auto-incrementing primary keys, replacing legacy SERIAL.
PostgreSQL native arrays and JSONB allow storing semi-structured and nested data cleanly.
JSONB supports high-speed querying with operators (->, ->>) and GIN indexing.
interview_takeaways: Mention that TEXT and VARCHAR share the same storage engine in PostgreSQL to demonstrate deep knowledge.
Insist on TIMESTAMPTZ for all global application event tables in system design questions.
Explain when JSONB is appropriate (polymorphic attributes, webhooks) vs when relational normalization is required.
common_mistakes: Using FLOAT/REAL for currency calculations, resulting in rounding errors
Using TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE for distributed event logging, causing timezone drift bugs
Using plain JSON instead of JSONB when planning to query or index keys inside the document
Using legacy SERIAL instead of GENERATED AS IDENTITY in modern PostgreSQL schemas
